**August 24, 1931 — a Monday**

The summer of 1931 was the moment the Great Depression became a global catastrophe.

In May, the Credit-Anstalt bank in Vienna — one of the largest and most important financial institutions in Central Europe — had failed. The collapse spread through the European banking system like a fire through connected rooms. German banks fell. British banks were threatened. By August, the contagion had reached London, the pound was under pressure, and international creditors were demanding the British government cut spending as the price of continued confidence. The Labour government of Ramsay MacDonald was caught between those demands and the reason the Labour Party existed. The Cabinet met repeatedly and couldn't agree. Ministers who had spent their careers fighting for unemployment benefits were being asked to cut them.

**On the exact day you were born**, MacDonald went to Buckingham Palace and resigned. King George V asked him to stay — not as a Labour Prime Minister, but as the head of a National Government: a coalition of Conservatives, Liberals, and a rump of Labour, assembled specifically to impose the austerity the creditors required. MacDonald accepted. The Labour Party immediately expelled him. Most of his Cabinet refused to serve under him. He spent the rest of his years in power leading a government dominated by his lifelong political opponents, sustained by votes from the party he had helped build against.

The British financial crisis of August 1931 was itself a consequence of a Viennese bank that had failed three months earlier. The Depression had become a system of connected failures, each triggering the next. You were born into the middle of that chain.

---

**Twenty-five days after your birth**, on September 18, officers of the Japanese Kwantung Army placed explosives on a railway line near Mukden in Manchuria and blamed Chinese saboteurs. The pretext was thin, the evidence obviously manufactured, and the invasion of Manchuria began immediately. The League of Nations would spend months investigating and issuing reports. Nothing was done. The lesson — that an aggressive military power with sufficient determination would not be stopped by international institutions — was filed away and remembered by other governments watching from Europe.

Seventeen months after your birth, Hitler became Chancellor of Germany.

---

**Fifty-five days after your birth**, on October 18, Thomas Edison died at 84.

Edison had been born in 1847, in a log house in Ohio, when Abraham Lincoln was practicing law in Illinois. He had invented the phonograph, developed a practical incandescent lightbulb, built the first electrical power grid, and contributed to the motion picture. The electrical infrastructure of modern civilization — the grid, the recorded sound, the moving image — bore his fingerprints. By the time you arrived in August 1931, he was already an old man in failing health, a figure from a previous century, the last inventor of his particular kind.

He died less than two months after you were born. The era he had built was what you were born into. The world that followed — transistors, satellites, microchips, the internet — he never saw and could not have predicted.

---

**The world of August 1931** had particular textures that are hard to recover now.

Radio was the dominant medium — not yet television, not yet the internet. Most American homes had a set. Network radio was the shared national experience: the same voices reaching farms in Nebraska and apartments in New York simultaneously. Talking pictures were barely four years old; "All Quiet on the Western Front" had come out the year before. Prohibition was still the law — it would last until December 1933.

In the Soviet Union, Stalin's forced collectivization was in its third year. The grain seizures from Ukrainian farms were accelerating. The famine that would kill millions — the Holodomor — was building. The scale of what was happening in Ukraine in 1931 would not be fully reckoned with for decades.

In London, Mahatma Gandhi was preparing to travel for the Round Table Conference on Indian independence — he would arrive three weeks after your birth, walking the streets of London in his dhoti, meeting with mill workers in Lancashire, becoming one of the most photographed figures in the world. Indian independence was still sixteen years away.

---

**Ninety-five years.**

The life expectancy at birth in the United States in 1931 was approximately 59 years. You have lived 36 years past the statistical expectation of the year you were born. That alone is a remarkable fact.

But consider the span of what those 95 years contain. You were born before: the New Deal, Social Security, widespread antibiotics, the atom bomb, the television in the living room, the computer, the polio vaccine, the interstate highway, the satellite, the internet, the smartphone. Every single one of those things arrived during your lifetime, most of them within memory.

You entered a world in financial collapse, with fascism rising in Europe, with the man who had built the electrical grid dying down the street, with an empire in Japan beginning the aggression that would engulf the Pacific, with a Soviet dictator starving his own people in secret. The Depression would last another decade. The war would kill 70 to 85 million people. And then, on the other side of all of that, came the longest sustained period of economic growth and relative peace in recorded history — the world you raised children in, built a life in, grew old in.

The summer of 1931 was as dark as the 20th century got before the darkness became something far worse. You were born at the beginning of it, and you are still here, on the other side.
